text: Welcome to Canada Tax Information for Newcomers. As a newcomer to Canada, you may need to file a Canadian income tax return. The tax year runs from January 1 to December 31. The deadline to file your return is April 30 of the following year. If you became a resident during the year, you only report income earned from the date you became a resident. The GST/HST credit is a tax-free quarterly payment that helps individuals and families with low and modest incomes. To receive it, you must file a tax return even if you have no income to report. The Canada Workers Benefit is a refundable tax credit to help individuals and families who are working and earning a low income. The Climate Action Incentive Payment is available to residents of Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Ontario, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island, and Newfoundland and Labrador. As a newcomer, apply for a Social Insurance Number as soon as possible.

Understanding Your T4 Slip — Statement of Remuneration Paid. Your employer issues a T4 slip showing how much employment income you received during the year and how much was withheld for income tax, CPP contributions, and EI premiums. You should receive your T4 by the last day of February for the previous tax year. If you worked for multiple employers, you will receive a T4 from each one. Box 14 shows your total employment income. Box 22 shows income tax deducted by your employer. Box 16 shows your CPP contributions. Box 18 shows your EI premiums paid. Box 24 shows EI insurable earnings. Box 26 shows CPP pensionable earnings. You need your T4 to file your tax return. If you lose it, get a copy from your employer or from My Account on the CRA website at canada.ca.

Canadian Tax Filing Deadlines. For most Canadians, the deadline to file your income tax return is April 30. If April 30 falls on a weekend, the deadline moves to the next business day. If you or your spouse are self-employed, the deadline to file is June 15. However, any balance owing is still due by April 30. Filing late results in a late-filing penalty of 5 percent of the balance owed, plus 1 percent for each full month your return is late, up to a maximum of 12 months. Even if you cannot pay what you owe, it is always better to file on time. Newcomers and students with no income should still file a return to access benefits and credits.

GST/HST Credit — Who is eligible and how to apply. The GST/HST credit is a tax-free quarterly payment from the CRA to help people with low or modest incomes offset the sales tax they pay. Payments are made in January, April, July, and October each year. You are automatically considered for the GST/HST credit when you file your income tax return. You do not need to apply separately. Even if you had no income, filing your return makes you eligible. As a newcomer, you may be eligible in the year you arrive in Canada. The amount depends on your family net income and the number of children. To receive the credit, you must be a Canadian resident and be 19 years of age or older, or have a spouse or common-law partner, or be a parent living with your child.

How to File Your Canadian Tax Return. There are two main paths to file your Canadian income tax return. The first path is filing yourself using certified tax software. NETFILE is the CRA online filing service — you use CRA-certified software to complete your return and submit it directly. The CRA maintains a list of free certified software options at canada.ca/netfile-software. The second path is working with a licensed tax professional who can file on your behalf, ensure accuracy, and maximize your credits and deductions. The Community Volunteer Income Tax Program offers free in-person help from trained volunteers for people with modest income and simple tax situations, available at locations across Canada. First-time filers should gather their T4 slips, Social Insurance Number, and date of entry into Canada before starting. For newcomers who are unsure about their situation, working with a professional is always the safer and often more beneficial option.

Tax Residency in Canada. Your tax obligations depend on your residency status for tax purposes, which is different from your immigration status. You become a Canadian resident for tax purposes when you establish significant residential ties to Canada — usually the date you moved here. Residential ties include having a home in Canada, a spouse or common-law partner, or dependants in Canada. As a newcomer, you file a tax return for the part of the year you were a Canadian resident. International students are generally considered Canadian residents if they live in Canada for more than 183 days in a calendar year. Work permit holders are generally considered residents while living and working in Canada.

RRSP — Registered Retirement Savings Plan Basics. An RRSP is a savings account registered with the Canadian government that lets you save for retirement while reducing your taxes today. Contributions are tax-deductible, meaning they reduce your taxable income. Your RRSP contribution room is 18 percent of your previous year earned income, up to the annual maximum. As a newcomer, you start building contribution room from your first year of Canadian income. You can contribute to your RRSP until December 31 of the year you turn 71. The RRSP contribution deadline is 60 days after December 31 — usually March 1. When you withdraw money from your RRSP, the amount is added to your income and taxed. Unused contribution room carries forward indefinitely.

TFSA — Tax-Free Savings Account for Newcomers. A TFSA is a registered account where your investments grow tax-free and withdrawals are never taxed. Unlike an RRSP, contributions do not reduce your taxable income, but all growth and withdrawals are tax-free. Every Canadian resident aged 18 or older earns TFSA contribution room each year. The annual limit changes each year — between 5,000 and 10,000 dollars per year since 2009. As a newcomer, you start accumulating TFSA room from the year you turn 18 and become a Canadian resident. You cannot use TFSA room from before you became a Canadian resident. A TFSA is often recommended for newcomers before an RRSP because withdrawals are flexible and tax-free at any time.

Canada Child Benefit — Tax-Free Monthly Payments for Families. The Canada Child Benefit is a tax-free monthly payment to eligible families to help with the cost of raising children under 18. To be eligible, you must be a Canadian resident and primarily responsible for raising the child. New residents can apply once they have lived in Canada for 18 months with a valid permit in the 19th month, or are a citizen or permanent resident. The amount depends on your family net income, number of children, and their ages. To receive the benefit, file your tax return. You can also apply using Form RC66. Payments are made on the 20th of each month.

Social Insurance Number — SIN for Newcomers. A Social Insurance Number is a nine-digit number you need to work in Canada or access government programs. Apply at a Service Canada office in person with your immigration documents such as your work permit, study permit, or permanent resident card. Processing is usually same day. Your SIN is confidential — only share it with your employer, your bank, and the CRA. You need your SIN to file your income tax return and to receive GST/HST credit, Canada Child Benefit, and Employment Insurance. Temporary residents receive a SIN starting with 9. This SIN is valid only while your immigration status is valid.

Self-Employment and Freelance Income in Canada. If you earn money working for yourself as a freelancer, consultant, or contractor, this is self-employment income. You must report all self-employment income on your tax return using Form T2125, Statement of Business or Professional Activities. Report your gross income and deduct eligible business expenses. Common deductible expenses include home office costs, phone and internet used for business, equipment, professional development, and advertising. Self-employed individuals pay both employee and employer portions of CPP contributions. If your self-employment income exceeds 30,000 dollars in any four consecutive quarters, you must register to collect GST or HST. The filing deadline is June 15, but taxes owing must be paid by April 30.

Tax Information for International Students in Canada. As an international student, you are generally a Canadian resident for tax purposes if you live in Canada for more than 183 days in a year and should file a tax return. The tuition tax credit lets you claim eligible tuition fees paid to a Canadian institution. You receive a T2202 form from your school showing eligible fees. If your tuition credit exceeds your tax owing, you can carry forward the unused amount or transfer up to 5,000 dollars to a parent or spouse. Students who worked part-time receive T4 slips and should include this income in their return. Even with low income, filing is important to access GST/HST credits and build RRSP room. Free tax help is available through the Community Volunteer Income Tax Program at many university campuses.

My CRA Account — Your Online Tax Portal. My Account is the CRA online portal where you can manage your tax affairs, view notices of assessment, check your RRSP and TFSA room, and set up direct deposit. To register, you need your SIN, date of birth, current postal code, and last year's tax return. From My Account you can view your tax return status, download T4 slips, check benefit payment dates, update your address and banking information, and set up direct deposit. Setting up direct deposit ensures your tax refund and benefit payments arrive within 5 to 10 business days. The MyCRA mobile app gives you access to key features on your phone.

Medical Expense Tax Credit in Canada. You can claim eligible medical expenses on your tax return to reduce taxes owed. Expenses must exceed the lesser of 3 percent of your net income or 2,635 dollars. Eligible expenses include prescription medications, dental care, vision care including glasses, medical devices prescribed by a doctor, ambulance services, and payments to licensed practitioners including doctors, dentists, nurses, and chiropractors. You can claim expenses for yourself, your spouse, and dependent children under 18. Keep all receipts for medical expenses. You cannot claim expenses reimbursed by insurance. Newcomers should keep receipts for all healthcare paid out of pocket, especially before employer benefits begin.

Moving Expenses Deduction. You may deduct eligible moving expenses if you moved to start a new job, run a business, or attend a university as a full-time student. Your new home must be at least 40 kilometers closer to your new work or school than your old home. Eligible expenses include transportation and storage of household items, travel expenses for you and your family, temporary living expenses for up to 15 days, costs to cancel a lease, and costs to maintain your old home while vacant and for sale. You can only deduct moving expenses from income earned at your new location. Keep all receipts and complete Form T1-M, Moving Expenses Deduction, on your tax return.

Rental Income in Canada. If you rent out a property or a room in your home, you must report this rental income on your tax return using Form T776, Statement of Real Estate Rentals. Report your gross rental income and deduct eligible expenses to calculate net rental income. Eligible expenses include mortgage interest, property taxes, insurance, maintenance and repairs, property management fees, advertising costs, and a portion of utilities if included in rent. You cannot deduct the principal portion of mortgage payments or personal expenses. If you rent part of your home, deduct a proportional share of expenses based on the rented area. Newcomers who own rental properties abroad must also report foreign rental income on their Canadian tax return.

Capital Gains in Canada. A capital gain occurs when you sell an asset for more than you paid for it. Common assets include stocks, mutual funds, cryptocurrency, and real estate other than your primary residence. In Canada, only 50 percent of your capital gain is included in your taxable income — this is the capital gains inclusion rate. Your principal residence is exempt from capital gains tax. Capital losses can only be used to offset capital gains and can be carried back three years or forward indefinitely. As a newcomer, when you become a Canadian resident, you are deemed to have acquired your assets at their fair market value on the date you became a resident. This sets your cost base for future capital gains. Cryptocurrency is treated as a commodity and buying and selling it can trigger capital gains.

Employment Insurance — EI Basics for Workers. Employment Insurance provides temporary income support to workers who lose their jobs, or cannot work due to illness, pregnancy, or caregiving. EI premiums are deducted automatically from your pay — see Box 18 of your T4. To qualify for regular EI benefits, you generally need between 420 and 700 insurable hours worked in the last 52 weeks. EI benefits are taxable income and must be reported on your tax return. You will receive a T4E slip showing EI benefits received. Self-employed individuals can voluntarily register for EI special benefits. Work permit holders who pay EI premiums are eligible for EI benefits and may continue to qualify even after their permit expires if they have enough hours.

Canada Pension Plan — CPP Contributions. The Canada Pension Plan is a mandatory pension program for workers in Canada outside Quebec. CPP contributions are deducted automatically from your pay if you are between 18 and 70 and earning employment income. Box 16 on your T4 shows your CPP contributions. When you retire, you receive a monthly CPP retirement pension based on how long you contributed and how much you earned. You can start CPP as early as age 60 with a reduced amount or as late as age 70 with an enhanced amount. As a newcomer, your Canadian CPP contributions count toward your future retirement pension. Self-employed individuals pay both the employer and employee portions of CPP, roughly double what employees pay.

Provincial and Territorial Income Tax in Canada. In Canada, you pay both federal income tax and provincial or territorial income tax. You pay provincial tax based on which province or territory you lived in on December 31 of the tax year. Each province has its own tax rates and brackets. Alberta has no provincial sales tax. Ontario has the Ontario Trillium Benefit combining energy, property tax, and sales tax credits. Quebec residents file a separate provincial tax return in addition to the federal return. All other provinces and territories use the same T1 General return for both federal and provincial taxes. For newcomers deciding where to live, provincial tax rates can significantly affect your take-home pay.

Ontario Trillium Benefit — Monthly Payments for Ontario Residents. The Ontario Trillium Benefit combines three tax credits: the Ontario Energy and Property Tax Credit, the Northern Ontario Energy Credit, and the Ontario Sales Tax Credit. The Ontario Sales Tax Credit helps low to moderate income individuals with sales tax paid. The Ontario Energy and Property Tax Credit helps with property tax and sales tax on home energy. Renters can claim the rental portion based on rent paid. To receive this benefit, file your Ontario tax return even if you had no income. The credit is calculated automatically when you indicate your rent or property tax paid. Payments are made monthly starting in July. Newcomers to Ontario should include rent paid on their tax return to maximize this benefit.

Reporting Foreign Income as a Canadian Resident. As a Canadian resident, you must report your worldwide income on your Canadian tax return. Foreign employment income, business income, pension income, and investment income must all be reported in Canadian dollars using the Bank of Canada exchange rate. Canada has tax treaties with many countries to prevent double taxation. You can claim a foreign tax credit for taxes paid to another country on income also taxed in Canada. Form T1135 must be filed if you held foreign property with a total cost over 100,000 Canadian dollars. Foreign pension income including social security from other countries must be reported. Newcomers should keep records of foreign income and taxes paid abroad for at least six years.

Setting Up Direct Deposit with the CRA. Direct deposit is the fastest way to receive your tax refund and government benefit payments. Set it up through My CRA Account online, the MyCRA mobile app, or by completing the direct deposit enrollment form. You will need your bank transit number, institution number, and account number — found at the bottom of a cheque or through online banking. All CRA payments including tax refunds, GST/HST credits, Canada Child Benefit, and other benefits go directly to your bank account. Refunds are deposited within 5 to 10 business days when you use direct deposit and NETFILE together. If you change banks, update your direct deposit information with the CRA immediately.

What to Do If You Owe Money to the CRA. If your tax return shows a balance owing, pay by April 30 to avoid interest charges. Interest on unpaid amounts is charged daily and compounds from May 1. Pay online through your bank using the payee name Canada Revenue Agency, at any bank branch, by mail, or through My Account. If you cannot pay the full amount, still file your return on time to avoid the late-filing penalty. Contact the CRA at 1-888-863-8657 to discuss a payment arrangement. The Voluntary Disclosures Program allows taxpayers with unfiled returns or unreported income to come forward with reduced penalties before the CRA contacts them. If you disagree with a CRA assessment, you have 90 days from the notice of assessment to file a formal objection.

Work From Home Deductions for Canadian Employees. If you worked from home, you may deduct home office expenses on your tax return. The detailed method allows you to deduct actual expenses based on the percentage of your home used for work, including rent, electricity, heating, internet, and maintenance. To use the detailed method, your employer must provide Form T2200, Declaration of Conditions of Employment. You can only deduct home office expenses against employment income from that employer. Supplies such as pens, paper, and printer ink can be deducted if required for work. Self-employed individuals have more flexibility and do not need a T2200.

First Time Home Buyer Incentives in Canada. The First Home Savings Account or FHSA lets you save up to 40,000 dollars tax-free to buy your first home. Annual contribution limit is 8,000 dollars. Contributions are tax-deductible like an RRSP and withdrawals for a qualifying home purchase are tax-free like a TFSA. The Home Buyers Plan allows you to withdraw up to 35,000 dollars from your RRSP tax-free to buy your first home, repayable over 15 years. The First-Time Home Buyers Tax Credit provides a 1,500 dollar non-refundable tax credit when you purchase a qualifying home. The GST/HST New Housing Rebate lets you recover part of the GST paid on a newly built home under 450,000 dollars. To qualify, neither you nor your spouse can have owned a home you lived in as principal residence in the past four years.

Understanding Your Notice of Assessment from the CRA. After you file your tax return, the CRA sends you a Notice of Assessment or NOA confirming they received and processed your return. It shows your total income, deductions, tax calculated, refund amount or balance owing, RRSP contribution room for next year, and TFSA contribution room. If the CRA made changes to your return, they explain them on the NOA. Keep your NOA in a safe place — you need it to register for My CRA Account and as proof of income. If you filed electronically using NETFILE, you usually receive your NOA within two weeks. You have 90 days from the date on your NOA to file a formal objection if you disagree with the assessment.

Canadian Federal Income Tax Brackets and Rates. Canada uses a progressive tax system where higher income is taxed at higher rates. Federal tax rates for 2024: the first 55,867 dollars is taxed at 15 percent; income between 55,867 and 111,733 dollars at 20.5 percent; between 111,733 and 154,906 dollars at 26 percent; between 154,906 and 220,000 dollars at 29 percent; income over 220,000 dollars at 33 percent. These are federal rates only — you also pay provincial tax. The basic personal amount is a non-refundable tax credit that reduces federal tax. For 2024, the basic personal amount is approximately 15,705 dollars. Everyone receives this credit regardless of income. Newcomers who arrive mid-year still apply the full basic personal amount.

What To Do If You Have Not Filed Tax Returns for Previous Years. If you have not filed tax returns for previous years, file them as soon as possible. The Voluntary Disclosures Program allows you to correct your tax affairs before the CRA contacts you. If you qualify, the CRA may waive penalties and reduce interest. To catch up on unfiled returns, gather your T4 slips and income documents for each missing year. You can request copies of tax slips from the CRA through My Account or by phone at 1-800-959-8281. Filing late returns may still result in refunds if you overpaid tax. You can generally go back up to 10 years to request a refund. Newcomers who did not know they were required to file can use the Voluntary Disclosures Program to file without penalty.

H&R Block Canada — Overview for Newcomers. H&R Block Canada is an independent tax preparation company with over 900 office locations across Canada. They offer both online software and in-person tax preparation services. TaxNorth has no affiliation or partnership with H&R Block Canada. This information is provided for educational purposes only. H&R Block Canada offers four online software tiers for the 2025 tax year: Free for basic T4 income and student returns; Deluxe at $29.99 for medical expenses and donations; Premier at $49.99 for capital gains and foreign income; and Self-Employed at $69.99 for freelancers and rental income. For in-person preparation at their offices, pricing starts at approximately $54.99 for simple returns and averages $99 or more for standard returns. They also offer an Expert Review add-on starting at $49.99 where a professional reviews your DIY return before filing. H&R Block offers a 25 percent discount for first-time filers who work with a tax expert. Their system handles newcomer situations including arrival dates for pro-rating federal and provincial tax credits. H&R Block is a private company and is not affiliated with the Canada Revenue Agency. For newcomers with complex situations involving multiple income sources, self-employment, or unfiled previous years, a licensed independent tax professional through TaxNorth may provide more personalized service than a software product.

TurboTax Canada — Overview for Newcomers. TurboTax Canada, owned by Intuit, is an online tax software platform with no physical office locations. TaxNorth has no affiliation or partnership with TurboTax Canada. This information is provided for educational purposes only. TurboTax Canada offers three service levels for the 2025 tax year: Do It Yourself ranging from $0 to approximately $70 depending on complexity; Expert Assist ranging from $70 to $150 which provides unlimited access to a tax expert who can review your screen and answer questions in real time; and Full Service ranging from $120 to $315 where a TurboTax-employed professional prepares and files your entire return. The free Do It Yourself tier covers basic T4 income, student credits, and RRSP contributions only. TurboTax offers a $20 rate for Expert Assist for users aged 25 and younger, which targets international students and young professionals. TurboTax has a dedicated newcomer section that addresses foreign income reporting, including Form T1135 which must be filed if you held foreign property worth more than $100,000 CAD at any point during the year. TurboTax is a digital-only platform and does not have physical offices in Canada. For newcomers who prefer in-person guidance or have complex situations, a licensed independent tax professional through TaxNorth provides personalized service that software cannot replicate.
